sections.authorBiography: Hermann Hesse was born on 2 July 1877 in Calw, in the German kingdom of Württemberg, into a family of Pietist Protestant missionaries with deep ties to India: his father, Johannes Hesse, had served with the Basel Mission there, his mother, Marie Gundert, was born in India, and his grandfather Hermann Gundert was a missionary scholar of Malayalam. As a teenager Hesse ran away from the Protestant seminary at Maulbronn and went through a severe personal crisis before training as a bookseller in Tübingen and Basel. His first success, Peter Camenzind (1904), let him live as a writer. During the First World War he published an appeal against nationalist hatred and was denounced in the German press; after the war, amid a breakdown of his marriage and his health, he moved to Montagnola in Switzerland and became a Swiss citizen in 1924. His major novels include Demian (1919), Siddhartha (1922), Steppenwolf (1927) and The Glass Bead Game (1943). He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946 and died in Montagnola on 9 August 1962.
sections.historicalContext: Siddhartha is set in India in the time of the Buddha (around the fifth century BCE), but it was written in Europe just after the First World War, when many young Germans had lost faith in the nation, the church and their parents' certainties. Hesse had grown up among books and stories about India, travelled in 1911 to Ceylon (Sri Lanka), Malaya and Sumatra, and read the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and Buddhist texts in translation. He was also influenced by psychoanalysis; he underwent analysis with a follower of Carl Jung around 1916–17. The novel is a European writer's imagined India: it uses Hindu and Buddhist ideas (Atman, Brahman, the Samanas, nirvana, Om, the cycle of Sansara) to tell a very personal story about finding one's own way.

publicationAndReception.publication: Hesse wrote the first part in 1919–20, then stopped for about a year and a half because, as he later explained, he could not write about a stage of experience he had not yet lived. The book appeared in 1922 from S. Fischer Verlag in Berlin, subtitled "an Indian poem"; the first part is dedicated to the French writer Romain Rolland and the second to Hesse's cousin Wilhelm Gundert, a scholar of Japan. An English translation by Hilda Rosner was published in the United States by New Directions in 1951.
publicationAndReception.then: In Germany in the 1920s the book was respected but not one of Hesse's bestsellers; readers knew him better for Demian. Some critics found its Indian setting exotic decoration for a European story of the self.
publicationAndReception.now: Siddhartha became a worldwide success after the 1951 English translation, especially in the 1960s, when the American counterculture embraced Hesse as a prophet of self-discovery and Eastern spirituality. It is now one of the most widely translated German novels and is taught in world literature and philosophy classes. Scholars today also discuss its limits: it is a Western, idealized picture of Indian religion, and its hero is not the Buddha but a seeker who rejects every teacher, including the Buddha.

sections.overview: Siddhartha, the gifted son of a Brahmin priest, leaves home with his friend Govinda to search for the truth about the self. He tries the life of the wandering ascetics, meets the Buddha, enters the world of a great city and a beautiful courtesan, and finally comes to a river and a ferryman. The book follows one man's whole life as he tests every path to wisdom.

mainThemes.note: what Siddhartha is looking for, and why no teacher can hand it to him.
Siddhartha learns from every person he meets but follows no one; ask what he learns and how.
the river becomes a teacher; watch how it is described each time it appears.
from friendship to the senses to a father's love; what does each kind of love teach him?
life and death, sin and holiness, stone and Buddha; the book's ending holds them together.

sections.whyItMatters: Students are at the age when Siddhartha leaves home, and the novel asks their questions: can you learn wisdom from teachers, or must you live it? It also lets classes examine how a Western writer imagined India, a useful lesson in reading cultural representation critically.

spoilerOverview.text: Siddhartha rejects the Buddha's teaching (though he reveres him), learns love from Kamala and business from Kamaswami, grows rich and empty, nearly drowns himself, and is renewed by the river. He becomes Vasudeva's fellow ferryman, meets Kamala again as she dies, and loses his son, who runs away. Listening to the river he hears the unity of all voices in Om; in old age he tells Govinda that wisdom cannot be taught, and Govinda sees all things in his face.

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “In the shade of the house, in the sunshine of the riverbank near the boats, in the shade of the Sal-wood forest, in the shade of the fig…” slowly and put it in my own words: Siddhartha grows up in shade and sunshine, near the river and the forest. Next, craft. I notice the repeated "in the shade," which creates a calm, chanting rhythm like a song. The strongest word is “shade”: it suggests protection and comfort, the sheltered life he will leave. Then, effect. What does this opening picture tell us about Siddhartha's early life? My answer: His childhood is peaceful and beautiful, yet the story will show he leaves it to search for something more; the river already appears.

segments.activity: Read the spoiler-free overview together and name the themes to track.
segments.script: What the book is about (no spoilers): Siddhartha, the gifted son of a Brahmin priest, leaves home with his friend Govinda to search for the truth about the self. He tries the life of the wandering ascetics, meets the Buddha, enters the world of a great city and a beautiful courtesan, and finally comes to a river and a ferryman. The book follows one man's whole life as he tests every path to wisdom. Themes to track: the search for the self: what Siddhartha is looking for, and why no teacher can hand it to him. teaching versus experience: Siddhartha learns from every person he meets but follows no one; ask what he learns and how. the river and time: the river becomes a teacher; watch how it is described each time it appears. love and attachment: from friendship to the senses to a father's love; what does each kind of love teach him? unity of opposites: life and death, sin and holiness, stone and Buddha; the book's ending holds them together.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Hesse, a German writer, studied Indian religions and published Siddhartha in 1922 after a visit to Asia. criticalVoices.quote: When as a mature man he travelled to the country of his desire he did not, indeed, solve the riddle of life; but the influence of Buddhism soon entered his thought, an influence by no means restricted to Siddhartha (1922) the beautiful story of a young Brahman’s search for the meaning of life on earth.
criticalVoices.speaker: Anders Österling, poet and Permanent Secretary of the Swedish Academy

criticalVoices.useNote: Context: the Nobel committee frames Siddhartha as a search, not an answer. Students predict what "solve the riddle of life" will mean for the hero.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this chapter, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Siddhartha.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Siddhartha: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Siddhartha has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to the search for self-knowledge.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Siddhartha. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this chapter, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the chapter on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the chapter to the search for self-knowledge.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the chapter quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Siddhartha.

objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the novel in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the chapter quizzes.
Students will write an argument with a clear claim, reasons and relevant evidence, scoring at least 80% on the unit test's short-answer scoring guides.

items.prompt: Claim: Siddhartha leaves the Buddha out of respect for the Buddha's own example. Explain how this evidence supports the claim: “Never before had Siddhartha venerated a person so much, never before had he loved a person as much as this one” (Gotama, paragraph 15).
items.expected: Although he says he had never "venerated a person so much," he argues the Buddha reached enlightenment by his own search, so following any teaching, even this one, would betray that example. The words “Never before had Siddhartha venerated a person so much, never before had he loved a person as much as this one” (Gotama, paragraph 15) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops teaching versus experience: Siddhartha argues the Buddha found enlightenment through his own experience, not through any teaching, so teaching cannot transmit it.

This develops the search for the self: Siddhartha asks where the Atman, the innermost self, can be found, and sees that the rituals and teachers have not found it. He "had started to nurse discontent in himself" despite universal love and asks "where, where was this Self," a question his father's rituals cannot answer.

The turning point of the chapter: discontent, not rebellion. The words “Siddhartha had started to nurse discontent in himself” (The Son of the Brahmin, paragraph 8) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops the search for the self: Siddhartha asks where the Atman, the innermost self, can be found, and sees that the rituals and teachers have not found it. He "had started to nurse discontent in himself" despite universal love and asks "where, where was this Self," a question his father's rituals cannot answer.

Siddhartha decides that the Samanas' path is only a way of escaping the self for a while, like a drunkard's escape. The words “With the Samanas” (With the Samanas, paragraph 11) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops teaching versus experience: Siddhartha decides that the Samanas' path is only a way of escaping the self for a while, like a drunkard's escape. He says what he learned "I could have learned more quickly and by simpler means," because meditation, like drink, only provides a temporary escape.

The goal of asceticism, stated in a list built on repetition. The words “to become empty, empty of thirst, empty of wishing, empty of dreams, empty of joy and sorrow” (With the Samanas, paragraph 3) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops teaching versus experience: Siddhartha decides that the Samanas' path is only a way of escaping the self for a while, like a drunkard's escape. He says what he learned "I could have learned more quickly and by simpler means," because meditation, like drink, only provides a temporary escape.

The Buddha's gracious response. The words “You’ve heard the teachings, O son of a Brahmin, and good for you that you’ve thought about it thus deeply” (Gotama, paragraph 36) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops teaching versus experience: Siddhartha argues the Buddha found enlightenment through his own experience, not through any teaching, so teaching cannot transmit it. Although he says he had never "venerated a person so much," he argues the Buddha reached enlightenment by his own search, so following any teaching, even this one, would betray that example.

The depth of his respect before his refusal. The words “Never before had Siddhartha venerated a person so much, never before had he loved a person as much as this one” (Gotama, paragraph 15) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops teaching versus experience: Siddhartha argues the Buddha found enlightenment through his own experience, not through any teaching, so teaching cannot transmit it. Although he says he had never "venerated a person so much," he argues the Buddha reached enlightenment by his own search, so following any teaching, even this one, would betray that example.

The diagnosis of everything he has tried so far: every discipline was a flight from the self. The words “I was afraid of myself, I was fleeing from myself” (Awakening, paragraph 4) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops the search for the self: Siddhartha realizes he never knew himself because "I was afraid of myself, I was fleeing from myself," and resolves to "learn from myself.". He realizes "I was afraid of myself, I was fleeing from myself," and now sees that "beautiful was the world, colourful was the world"; but in the same moment he stands "alone like a star in the sky," because he no longer belongs to any group.

Inverted word order and repetition give the line the rhythm of a hymn: the world itself is now sacred. The words “Beautiful was the world, colourful was the world, strange and mysterious was the world” (Awakening, paragraph 7) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops the search for the self: Siddhartha realizes he never knew himself because "I was afraid of myself, I was fleeing from myself," and resolves to "learn from myself.". He realizes "I was afraid of myself, I was fleeing from myself," and now sees that "beautiful was the world, colourful was the world"; but in the same moment he stands "alone like a star in the sky," because he no longer belongs to any group.

Siddhartha's three skills: everything his ascetic life gave him, offered as currency in the city. The words “I can think. I can wait. I can fast” (Kamala, paragraph 42) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops teaching versus experience: after rejecting every spiritual teacher, Siddhartha chooses a teacher of the senses; he still learns, but now through experience. The ferryman says "This too, I have learned from the river: everything is coming back! You too, Samana, will come back," naming the river as his teacher and predicting Siddhartha's return long before it happens.

Vasudeva's prophecy; the river is already a teacher. The words “This too, I have learned from the river: everything is coming back” (Kamala, paragraph 11) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops teaching versus experience: after rejecting every spiritual teacher, Siddhartha chooses a teacher of the senses; he still learns, but now through experience. The ferryman says "This too, I have learned from the river: everything is coming back! You too, Samana, will come back," naming the river as his teacher and predicting Siddhartha's return long before it happens.

The simile that shows how he sees others. The words “Most people, Kamala, are like a falling leaf, which is blown and is turning around through the air, and wavers, and tumbles to the ground” (With the Childlike People, paragraph 42) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops love and attachment: Kamala says "perhaps people of our kind can't love. The childlike people can": both are detached, and that is their limit. He compares most people to "a falling leaf" and himself, implicitly, to the stars, and Kamala sees the cost: "perhaps people of our kind can't love. The childlike people can.".

Kamala says "perhaps people of our kind can't love. The childlike people can": both are detached, and that is their limit. The words “With the Childlike People” (With the Childlike People, paragraph 47) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops love and attachment: Kamala says "perhaps people of our kind can't love. The childlike people can": both are detached, and that is their limit. He compares most people to "a falling leaf" and himself, implicitly, to the stars, and Kamala sees the cost: "perhaps people of our kind can't love. The childlike people can.".

The dream that wakes him. The words “Kamala owned a small, rare singing bird in a golden cage. Of this bird he dreamt” (Sansara, paragraph 10) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops love and attachment: the senses, pursued without love, become a cycle of craving: this is Sansara. He dreams that the bird in its "golden cage" has become mute, and after he leaves, Kamala "opened the door of the cage, took the bird out and let it fly," marking his release.

The turn after Om; his first smile since the city. The words “Now, Siddhartha smiled” (By the River, paragraph 22) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops the search for the self: Siddhartha sees that he had to go through folly to kill the proud Brahmin and Samana within him. Full of Sansara "like a sponge sucks up water until it is full," he wants to die, but after the Om and his sleep "Siddhartha smiled," and he judges even his years in the city as a necessary part of the path.

Simile for the saturation of his worldly life. The words “Deeply, he had been entangled in Sansara, he had sucked up disgust and death from all sides into his body, like a sponge sucks up water…” (By the River, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops the search for the self: Siddhartha sees that he had to go through folly to kill the proud Brahmin and Samana within him. Full of Sansara "like a sponge sucks up water until it is full," he wants to die, but after the Om and his sleep "Siddhartha smiled," and he judges even his years in the city as a necessary part of the path.

Siddhartha sees that he had to go through folly to kill the proud Brahmin and Samana within him. The words “By the River” (By the River, paragraph 1) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops the search for the self: Siddhartha sees that he had to go through folly to kill the proud Brahmin and Samana within him. Full of Sansara "like a sponge sucks up water until it is full," he wants to die, but after the Om and his sleep "Siddhartha smiled," and he judges even his years in the city as a necessary part of the path.

The river's lesson about time. The words “that the river is everywhere at once, at the source and at the mouth, at the waterfall, at the ferry, at the rapids, in the sea, in the…” (The Ferryman, paragraph 34) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops the river and time: the river is "everywhere at once"; there is no time, only the present. He learns that "the river is everywhere at once," and concludes, "Nothing was, nothing will be; everything is," so his past selves are not lost but present.

The river is "everywhere at once"; there is no time, only the present. The words “The Ferryman” (The Ferryman, paragraph 34) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops the river and time: the river is "everywhere at once"; there is no time, only the present. He learns that "the river is everywhere at once," and concludes, "Nothing was, nothing will be; everything is," so his past selves are not lost but present.

The inner voice that makes him a ferryman. The words “Love this water! Stay near it! Learn from it” (The Ferryman, paragraph 2) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops the river and time: the river is "everywhere at once"; there is no time, only the present. He learns that "the river is everywhere at once," and concludes, "Nothing was, nothing will be; everything is," so his past selves are not lost but present.

Kamala's old words haunt him. The words “You cannot love” (The Son, paragraph 17) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops love and attachment: a father's love becomes his "final wound.". Vasudeva asks whether he committed "foolish acts in order to spare your son from committing them too," reminding him that he, too, left his father.

Vasudeva's question: each must find his own way. The words “Would you actually believe that you had committed your foolish acts in order to spare your son from committing them too” (The Son, paragraph 14) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops love and attachment: a father's love becomes his "final wound.". Vasudeva asks whether he committed "foolish acts in order to spare your son from committing them too," reminding him that he, too, left his father.

The climax. The words “then the great song of the thousand voices consisted of a single word, which was Om: the perfection” (Om, paragraph 17) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops unity of opposites: all voices are one. Only after his "final wound" does "the great song of the thousand voices" consist "of a single word, which was Om: the perfection," and he sees the same "oneness" in Vasudeva's smiling face.

Govinda's problem. The words “Searching means: having a goal. But finding means: being free, being open, having no goal” (Govinda, paragraph 7) are the evidence: their wording makes this point in the text itself. This develops teaching versus experience: knowledge can be taught, wisdom cannot. Siddhartha tells Govinda that "wisdom cannot be passed on" and that "searching means: having a goal," which is Govinda's obstacle; Govinda's understanding comes only when he kisses Siddhartha's forehead and sees, rather than hears.

prompts.text: Analyze how Hermann Hesse develops the search for self-knowledge across Siddhartha. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Siddhartha and argue how its meaning changes over the novel and why that change matters to experience versus teaching.
Analyze a central character's choices in Siddhartha. Argue whether the novel judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.
Two readers disagree about whether Siddhartha finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of the unity of all things. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

criticalVoices.quote: He has literally, once and more than once, stood on the magic borderland where everything is affirmed, where not only the remotest thought is true, but also the contrary of such thought.
criticalVoices.speaker: Hermann Hesse, author (essay written 1919, while Siddhartha was in progress)
criticalVoices.source: "Thoughts on The Idiot of Dostoevsky," trans. Stephen Hudson, The Dial 73.2 (August 1922), pp. 199-204; German original in Blick ins Chaos (1920), essay text (on Prince Myshkin)
criticalVoices.useNote: Author's-own-lens: Hesse says this of Dostoevsky's Myshkin, but it is the creed of "Govinda" ("the opposite of every truth is just as true"). Does the novel present this borderland as wisdom, or only as one man's experience?

criticalVoices.quote: Whosoever considers Spirit and Nature, Spirit and Freedom, Good and Evil as interchangeable, if only for a moment, is the deadliest foe of every order of civilization.
criticalVoices.speaker: Hermann Hesse, author (essay written 1919, while Siddhartha was in progress)
criticalVoices.source: "Thoughts on The Idiot of Dostoevsky," trans. Stephen Hudson, The Dial 73.2 (August 1922), pp. 199-204; German original in Blick ins Chaos (1920), essay text
criticalVoices.useNote: Objection to answer: Hesse states the society's fear himself. Does Siddhartha's final vision (the river, Govinda's kiss) make him civilization's "foe," or does the novel reject that charge? A ready-made counter-argument paragraph.
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Final paper Prompt 4: answer the strongest objection, namely that unity dissolves moral order.
